name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q01 - Octet rule exceptions and resonance canonical forms

questiontext.text:
Consider the following three statements regarding the octet rule and resonance:

Statement I: In \(\mathrm{SF}_6\), the central sulphur atom is surrounded by \(12\) valence electrons, representing an expanded octet.

Statement II: Nitric oxide (\(\mathrm{NO}\)) and nitrogen dioxide (\(\mathrm{NO}_2\)) are odd-electron molecules in which the octet rule is not satisfied for all atoms.

Statement III: The canonical structures of a resonance hybrid have real independent existence and remain in dynamic equilibrium with one another.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the octet rule, atoms combine by transferring or sharing valence electrons to attain eight electrons in their valence shell. However, this rule has exceptions such as incomplete octets, odd-electron species, and expanded octets in elements of the third period and beyond where \(d\) orbitals are available for bonding. Separately, resonance describes molecules that cannot be represented by a single Lewis structure, using multiple hypothetical canonical forms to depict a single resonance hybrid.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Expanded Octet in \(\mathrm{SF}_6\)
Sulphur belongs to the third period and has \(3s\), \(3p\), and \(3d\) orbitals available for bonding. In \(\mathrm{SF}_6\), the central sulphur atom forms six single covalent bonds with six fluorine atoms. Since each covalent bond consists of \(2\) shared electrons, there are \(6 \times 2 = 12\) valence electrons around the central sulphur atom. Because this exceeds eight electrons, \(\mathrm{SF}_6\) is a valid example of an expanded octet.

Step 3: Evaluation of Odd-Electron Molecules
In \(\mathrm{NO}\), nitrogen contributes \(5\) valence electrons and oxygen contributes \(6\), giving a total of \(11\) valence electrons. In \(\mathrm{NO}_2\), nitrogen contributes \(5\) and two oxygen atoms contribute \(12\), giving \(17\) valence electrons. Because the total number of valence electrons is odd, it is impossible for every atom in these molecules to achieve a complete octet of eight electrons.

Step 4: Evaluation of Resonance Canonical Forms
Canonical structures (or resonance forms) are theoretical representations drawn when a single Lewis structure fails to match experimentally observed bond parameters. These canonical forms have no real existence, the molecule does not spend fractions of time in different canonical forms, and there is no dynamic equilibrium between them (unlike tautomeric forms). Instead, the molecule has a single actual structure represented by the resonance hybrid.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The claims regarding the expanded octet of \(12\) electrons in \(\mathrm{SF}_6\) and the failure of the octet rule in odd-electron molecules \(\mathrm{NO}\) and \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) are correct, whereas the claim that canonical structures have real existence and exist in dynamic equilibrium is incorrect.

answer.text: Statement I, Statement II and Statement III are all correct
Only Statement I and Statement II are correct
Only Statement II and Statement III are correct
Only Statement I and Statement III are correct

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q02 - Dipole moment of ammonia and VSEPR repulsions

questiontext.text:
Read the following three statements carefully:

Statement I: Although fluorine is more electronegative than nitrogen, the resultant dipole moment of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) is greater than that of \(\mathrm{NF}_3\).

Statement II: In \(\mathrm{NH}_3\), the orbital dipole due to the lone pair acts in the direction opposite to the resultant dipole moment of the three \(\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{H}\) bonds.

Statement III: According to VSEPR theory, the repulsive interaction between electron pairs around a central atom decreases in the order: \(\text{lone pair}-\text{lone pair} > \text{lone pair}-\text{bond pair} > \text{bond pair}-\text{bond pair}\).

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For polyatomic molecules, the net dipole moment \(\mu\) is the vector sum of individual bond dipoles and any orbital dipole arising from lone pairs on the central atom. According to VSEPR theory, lone pairs are localised on the central atom and occupy more space than bonding pairs shared between two nuclei, which governs the relative magnitudes of electron-pair repulsions.

Step 2: Comparison of Dipole Moments in \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) and \(\mathrm{NF}_3\)
Both \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) and \(\mathrm{NF}_3\) have a trigonal pyramidal geometry with one lone pair on the nitrogen atom. Experimentally, the resultant dipole moment of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) is \(4.90 \times 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\ m}\) (\(1.47\ \mathrm{D}\)), which is significantly greater than that of \(\mathrm{NF}_3\) at \(0.80 \times 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{C\ m}\) (\(0.23\ \mathrm{D}\)), even though fluorine is more electronegative than nitrogen. Thus, the comparison stating that \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) has a greater dipole moment than \(\mathrm{NF}_3\) is correct.

Step 3: Direction of Orbital Dipole and Bond Dipoles in \(\mathrm{NH}_3\)
In \(\mathrm{NH}_3\), nitrogen is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the three \(\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{H}\) bond dipoles point towards nitrogen. The orbital dipole due to the lone pair also points away from the nitrogen atom in the same general direction as the resultant of the three \(\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{H}\) bond dipoles, reinforcing the net dipole moment. In contrast, in \(\mathrm{NF}_3\), the \(\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{F}\) bond dipoles point towards fluorine (away from nitrogen), opposing the lone-pair orbital dipole and reducing the net dipole moment. Therefore, claiming that the lone-pair orbital dipole opposes the \(\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{H}\) bond dipoles in \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) is incorrect.

Step 4: VSEPR Repulsion Order
Because lone-pair electron clouds are held by only one nucleus and spread out over a larger volume than bond pairs, repulsions involving lone pairs are stronger. Consequently, the repulsive interaction decreases in the order \(\text{lp}-\text{lp} > \text{lp}-\text{bp} > \text{bp}-\text{bp}\), which is a core postulate of VSEPR theory.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Only the claims that \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) has a higher dipole moment than \(\mathrm{NF}_3\) and that VSEPR electron-pair repulsions follow the order \(\text{lp}-\text{lp} > \text{lp}-\text{bp} > \text{bp}-\text{bp}\) are correct, while the claim about opposing dipole directions in \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) is incorrect.

answer.text: Only Statement I and Statement II are correct
Only Statement II and Statement III are correct
Only Statement I and Statement III are correct
Statement I, Statement II and Statement III are all correct

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_CHEMICALBONDING_MCQ_Q03 - Molecular orbital theory and trigonal bipyramidal geometry

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the following three statements regarding molecular orbital theory and hybridisation:

Statement I: The double bond in the \(\mathrm{C}_2\) molecule consists of two \(\pi\) bonds because four electrons occupy the \(\pi 2p_x\) and \(\pi 2p_y\) molecular orbitals, resulting in a diamagnetic molecule with a bond order of \(2\).

Statement II: For homonuclear diatomic molecules such as \(\mathrm{B}_2\), \(\mathrm{C}_2\), and \(\mathrm{N}_2\), the energy of the \(\sigma 2p_z\) molecular orbital is higher than that of the degenerate \(\pi 2p_x\) and \(\pi 2p_y\) molecular orbitals, which accounts for the paramagnetic nature of \(\mathrm{B}_2\).

Statement III: In \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) (\(sp^3d\) hybridisation), the two axial \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Cl}\) bonds are slightly longer and weaker than the three equatorial \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Cl}\) bonds due to greater repulsive interactions from the equatorial bond pairs.

Which of the above statements are correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
We are evaluating three molecular bonding properties: (a) the electronic configuration, bond order, magnetic nature, and \(\pi\)-bond character of \(\mathrm{C}_2\) (\(12\) electrons); (b) the molecular orbital energy ordering for \(\mathrm{B}_2\) (\(10\) electrons), \(\mathrm{C}_2\), and \(\mathrm{N}_2\); and (c) the axial versus equatorial bond lengths and strengths in \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\) with \(sp^3d\) hybridisation.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In Molecular Orbital (MO) theory, bond order is given by \(\text{Bond order} = \frac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)\), where \(N_b\) is the number of electrons in bonding MOs and \(N_a\) is the number in antibonding MOs. A species is paramagnetic if it has one or more unpaired electrons and diamagnetic if all electrons are paired. For \(\mathrm{B}_2\), \(\mathrm{C}_2\), and \(\mathrm{N}_2\), \(2s\)-\(2p\) mixing places \(\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y\) below \(\sigma 2p_z\): \[\sigma 1s < \sigma^* 1s < \sigma 2s < \sigma^* 2s < (\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y) < \sigma 2p_z < (\pi^* 2p_x = \pi^* 2p_y) < \sigma^* 2p_z\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working for \(\mathrm{C}_2\) and \(\mathrm{B}_2\)
For \(\mathrm{C}_2\) (\(12\) electrons), the configuration is \(\mathrm{KK}(\sigma 2s)^2(\sigma^* 2s)^2(\pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2)\). Counting valence and core bonding/antibonding electrons gives \(N_b = 8\) and \(N_a = 4\), so \(\text{Bond order} = \frac{1}{2}(8 - 4) = 2\). Since all four highest-energy electrons are paired in \(\pi 2p_x\) and \(\pi 2p_y\), \(\mathrm{C}_2\) is diamagnetic and its double bond consists of two \(\pi\) bonds. For \(\mathrm{B}_2\) (\(10\) electrons), the configuration is \(\mathrm{KK}(\sigma 2s)^2(\sigma^* 2s)^2(\pi 2p_x^1 = \pi 2p_y^1)\). Because \(\sigma 2p_z\) lies higher in energy than the degenerate \(\pi 2p_x\) and \(\pi 2p_y\) orbitals, Hund's rule places one unpaired electron in each \(\pi 2p\) orbital, making \(\mathrm{B}_2\) paramagnetic.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working for \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\)
In \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\), phosphorus undergoes \(sp^3d\) hybridisation to form a trigonal bipyramidal geometry. Three \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Cl}\) bonds lie in the equatorial plane at \(120^\circ\) to each other, while two axial \(\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Cl}\) bonds lie perpendicular to this plane at \(90^\circ\) to the equatorial bonds. Because the axial bond pairs experience greater repulsive interaction from the three equatorial bond pairs at \(90^\circ\), the axial bonds are slightly longer and consequently slightly weaker than the equatorial bonds.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
All three chemical relationships—the two-\(\pi\)-bond diamagnetic structure of \(\mathrm{C}_2\) with bond order \(2\), the higher energy of \(\sigma 2p_z\) relative to \(\pi 2p_x/\pi 2p_y\) causing paramagnetism in \(\mathrm{B}_2\), and the longer, weaker axial bonds in \(\mathrm{PCl}_5\)—are fully consistent with MO theory and hybridisation principles. Hence, all three statements are correct.

answer.text: Only Statement I and Statement II are correct
Only Statement II and Statement III are correct
Only Statement I and Statement III are correct
Statement I, Statement II and Statement III are all correct
